items.title: One year in: How Microsoft Research Asia – Singapore is advancing research, partnership and talent for real-world impact
items.content: On July 24, 2025, Microsoft Research Asia – Singapore (MSRA – Singapore) opened its doors as Microsoft’s first research lab in Southeast Asia. The launch built on more than two decades of collaboration between Microsoft Research Asia and Singapore’s universities, research institutes, and government agencies. It marked a shift to a closer, more integrated relationship aimed at supporting Singapore’s innovation ecosystem and advancing the development and beneficial use of AI. “When we established Microsoft Research Asia — Singapore one year ago, our vision was not simply to open another research lab. It was to build a bridge connecting Microsoft’s frontier AI research with Singapore’s world-class universities, forward-thinking government agencies, and dynamic industry ecosystem. One year in, what gives me the greatest confidence is not just the research we have produced, but the depth of partnership we have built. That is the foundation on which lasting impact is built.”— Dr. Lidong Zhou, corporate vice president at Microsoft and managing director of Microsoft Research Asia Established in 1998, MSRA has a presence in Beijing, Shanghai, Vancouver, and Tokyo, along with Singapore. The Singapore lab strengthens the collaboration with local partners and extends the scientific and societal impact of Microsoft’s global research community.  Over the past year, the Singapore lab has grown its team, deepened partnerships, and explored how frontier AI research can create real-world value. Guided by its mission to advance frontier AI for humanity, its work spans four pillars: next-generation AI models and agentic systems, domain-specific AI for real-world impact, AI-native research practices, and ecosystem and talent development. From frontier research to real-world impact – and back Research has its greatest impact when it moves beyond the laboratory into practice: in health and medicine, enterprises, and the daily operations of organizations solving real problems. MSRA – Singapore aims to do just that through a two-way exchange: partners bring domain expertise, real-world data, and operational challenges, while the lab contributes frontier research and engineering capabilities. Together, they translate fundamental advances into practical solutions, while surfacing new questions that feed back into research in a kind of research-to-impact flywheel. Advances in AI foundations enable more capable models and agentic systems that can reason, plan, use tools, and collaborate with people. These capabilities create new opportunities for AI-native innovation. In turn, real-world applications reveal limitations and generate new questions, feeding insights back into foundational research and sustaining a continuous cycle of discovery, application, and learning. Healthcare offers an early example of the lab’s research-to-impact model. Research on multimodal healthcare AI and self-evolving diagnostic agents is deployed and extended through partnerships across Singapore’s healthcare ecosystem. The lab is collaborating on multimodal and agentic AI approaches to support clinical decision-making, unlock insights from complex medical data, and advance research in disease diagnosis, risk assessment, and personalized care, with the longer-term goal of enabling meaningful real-world use. Beyond healthcare, the lab is working with organizations across financial services, education, and technology to explore how frontier AI can address sector-specific needs and operational challenges. “Over the past year, the lab has become an integral part of both Microsoft’s local ecosystem and Singapore’s broader innovation community. Its progress demonstrates the value of establishing a sustained research presence in Singapore.”— Wee Luen Chia, managing director, Microsoft Singapore Singapore has made AI a national priority through its National AI Strategy 2.0 (opens in new tab), which focuses on deploying industry-transforming AI, advancing frontier research in AI foundations, and developing responsible, socially beneficial applications. These priorities span areas including healthcare, education, finance, and Smart Nation (opens in new tab) services. MSRA – Singapore’s research portfolio aligns with these priorities, with a particular focus on building AI systems that are reliable and trustworthy across Southeast Asian contexts.  The Singapore Economic Development Board (EDB) has been a foundational partner. It supported the lab’s establishment and continues to support joint PhD training through the Industrial Postgraduate Programme (IPP). The relationship has since grown into strategic collaboration. In February 2026, EDB co-hosted an Executive Roundtable on AI in Logistics and Transportation, bringing together more than ten regional industry leaders to explore sectoral challenges. “Singapore is building deep research capabilities to push the boundaries of AI and other frontier technologies. Microsoft Research Asia – Singapore is an important partner in this effort. Since its launch in 2025, the lab has brought Microsoft’s global research expertise closer to our ecosystem, partnering academia, industry, and government to advance frontier AI research and translate it into real-world applications in areas such as healthcare. MSRA is also developing the next generation of AI research talent who can create meaningful impact for our economy and society.”— Low Jin Yong, senior vice president and co-head, Digital Industry Singapore Government engagement extends beyond EDB. In July 2025, IMDA (opens in new tab) co-hosted Microsoft Research Asia Singapore Day (opens in new tab) — Advancing Industrial AI, a full-day event spanning healthcare AI, interactive world simulators, AI agents, and societal AI. MSRA – Singapore has also engaged with the Ministry of Trade and Industry and the Ministry of Health.  From enduring partnerships to shared discovery In addition to its deep ties with government agencies, MSRA has built strong connections with Singapore’s academic community, supporting more than 75 research projects with Singapore institutions since 2004. The opening of the Singapore lab has brought new engagements, with nine new projects in its first year with National University of Singapore (NUS) and Nanyang Technological University, Singapore (NTU) across healthcare AI, robotics, AI systems, and multi-agent systems.  A landmark example is the five-year Framework Research Agreement (opens in new tab) with NUS, announced in 2025, which provides a platform for joint AI research, talent development, and academic exchange. It defines shared research priorities in healthcare, societal AI, spatial intelligence, and data-intensive computing alongside an annual NUS–MSRA Academic Symposium that brings researchers from both organizations together to shape the collaboration agenda.  “This partnership creates new opportunities for frontier research, talent development, and knowledge exchange, strengthening connections across academia, industry, and the broader innovation ecosystem.”— Professor Liu Bin, deputy president (Research and Technology), National University of Singapore The collaboration is already producing concrete research across several frontier areas. NUS Assistant Professor Mike Shou and MSRA’s Xinxing Xu are developing unified multimodal AI for healthcare. NUS assistant professor Yang You and MSRA distinguished scientist Furu Wei are studying systems foundations for diffusion-based language models. NUS assistant professor Jialin Li is working with MSRA on rigorous distributed agreement in multi-agent systems and verifiable machine learning systems. “Whether during my visit to the Systems Research Group in Beijing or through our ongoing collaborations, I have been impressed by how deeply MSRA researchers engage with difficult problems and how openly they exchange ideas. For young faculty and students, it is a rare environment to explore ambitious ideas.“— Jialin Li, Sung Kah Kay Assistant Professor, School of Computing, National University of Singapore, MSRA StarTrack Scholar The NUS–Microsoft Research Asia AI Summer School has reached more than 300 students since its launch in 2025, attracting participants from Singapore, Southeast Asia, and beyond. Through three days of lectures, hands-on workshops, and small-group discussions, the program creates a forum for researchers and students to engage with emerging AI questions and scholars shaping the field. The 2025 program featured a keynote by Doug Burger, technical fellow and corporate vice president of Microsoft, on the AI revolution. Ahead of the 2026 Summer School, Lidong Zhou delivered a lecture on system intelligence, helping frame the conversations that followed.  “I have seen the NUS–MSRA partnership grow through sustained collaboration in AI research and talent development. What makes this partnership especially meaningful is the opportunity to bring together researchers and students from both communities to learn from one another, pursue new ideas, and create lasting impact together.”— Tulika Mitra, dean, NUS School of Computing Beyond NUS, Microsoft Research Asia — Singapore has built connections across Singapore’s research community, including with NTU, Singapore Management University (SMU) (opens in new tab), Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR), and other institutions. Research arising from these partnerships has already been published at leading venues, including the International Conference on Learning Representations (opens in new tab) (ICLR) and the Conference on Language Modeling (opens in new tab) (COLM).  From early exposure to research leadership: Cultivating Singapore’s next generation of AI talent For Microsoft Research Asia, talent development is not a standalone program but a long-term investment in Singapore’s research and innovation capacity, supporting a comprehensive talent pipeline spanning internships, joint PhD supervision, visiting scholar programs, and fellowship initiatives. Through these opportunities, students and early-career researchers gain access to world-class mentorship, a curiosity-driven culture, frontier research challenges, and a global network connecting academia, industry, and real-world applications. What makes this model distinctive is its continuity. Students may engage with Microsoft Research Asia through workshops or summer schools, gain hands-on experience through its flagship research initiative, Microsoft Research Asia Stars of Tomorrow Internship Program, or pursue doctoral research through joint PhD programs. Some participants later return as faculty collaborators, mentors, or research leaders. Together, these programs form a connected pathway that supports researchers at successive stages of development.  The IPP represents a sustained form of collaboration, enabling PhD students to conduct long-term research under joint mentorship from academia and industry. Qiming Huang, the first IPP student at MSRA — Singapore, is co-supervised by NUS professor Mike Shou and MSRA researcher Xinxing Xu. Through the program, Huang worked closely with researchers from both institutions, gaining exposure to academic rigor and industry-driven research. At CVPR 2026 (opens in new tab), one of the world’s leading conferences in AI and computer vision, Qiming Huang’s paper on RobotSeg – a foundation model for robot segmentation in image and video – was selected for an oral presentation. “Working alongside researchers from both Microsoft Research Asia and NUS changed how I approach AI research. Beyond technical guidance, I learned to frame ambitious questions, collaborate across disciplines, and think about the real-world impact of research— Qiming Huang, IPP student from National University of Singapore NTU assistant professor Jianfei Yang, embodies the continuous collaborative opportunities enabled by Microsoft Research Asia. As a student, Yang’s team won the Beauty of Programming competition, an experience that inspired him to pursue a PhD and begin an academic career. Over the years, he watched many of his classmates and close friends grow into outstanding researchers through MSRA programs. Today, he collaborates with MSRA researchers in robotics and jointly supervises students through the IPP, creating for the next generation the same opportunities that inspired his own journey. “Although I never interned at Microsoft Research Asia myself, it always felt close. Having the opportunity to work alongside a research lab that inspired so many researchers of my generation, and now to co-mentor students together, is both meaningful and rewarding.”— Jianfei Yang, assistant professor, director of Multimodal embodied AI and Robotic Systems (MARS) Lab, Nanyang Technological University NTU associate professor Ziwei Liu, himself a former MSRA intern, recently saw one of his students become the only Asia-based recipient of the Microsoft Research global Fellowship award for 2025–2026. “As a former intern, I have seen how an environment that brings together world-class researchers, open scientific exchange, and ambitious young talent can shape the next generation of researchers. It is especially meaningful to see my own students now benefit from these opportunities.” — Ziwei Liu, associate professor, College of Computing and Data Science, Nanyang Technological University The Stars of Tomorrow Internship Program has engaged more than 90 students from Singapore-based institutions over the years. For many students, these internships serve as a gateway to frontier research and help bridge the gap between academic study and real-world innovation. For exceptional doctoral students, the Microsoft Research Asia Fellowship provides another pathway for growth, recognition, mentorship, and access to Microsoft’s global research community. Since the program began, 13 students from Singapore-based universities have received the fellowship, many of whom have gone on to become professors, industry research leaders, and technology entrepreneurs around the world. The next phase: Scaling what works As Microsoft Research Asia — Singapore enters its second year, the focus is shifting from building foundations to scaling the strongest models of collaboration and demonstrating their impact more broadly. One year ago, the lab opened with a mission to advance frontier AI in close partnership with the ecosystem around it. That mission is already taking shape through joint research, talent development, and the first partnerships connecting lab work to real-world challenges. The year ahead is about scaling what works. By deepening these connections, Microsoft Research Asia — Singapore can bring more frontier research into practice and create meaningful value for Singapore, the wider region, industry, and society.  Opens in a new tabThe post One year in: How Microsoft Research Asia – Singapore is advancing research, partnership and talent for real-world impact appeared first on Microsoft Research.

MSRA is also developing the next generation of AI research talent who can create meaningful impact for our economy and society.”— Low Jin Yong, senior vice president and co-head, Digital Industry Singapore Government engagement extends beyond EDB. In July 2025, IMDA (opens in new tab) co-hosted Microsoft Research Asia Singapore Day (opens in new tab) — Advancing Industrial AI, a full-day event spanning healthcare AI, interactive world simulators, AI agents, and societal AI. MSRA – Singapore has also engaged with the Ministry of Trade and Industry and the Ministry of Health.  From enduring partnerships to shared discovery In addition to its deep ties with government agencies, MSRA has built strong connections with Singapore’s academic community, supporting more than 75 research projects with Singapore institutions since 2004. The opening of the Singapore lab has brought new engagements, with nine new projects in its first year with National University of Singapore (NUS) and Nanyang Technological University, Singapore (NTU) across healthcare AI, robotics, AI systems, and multi-agent systems.  A landmark example is the five-year Framework Research Agreement (opens in new tab) with NUS, announced in 2025, which provides a platform for joint AI research, talent development, and academic exchange. It defines shared research priorities in healthcare, societal AI, spatial intelligence, and data-intensive computing alongside an annual NUS–MSRA Academic Symposium that brings researchers from both organizations together to shape the collaboration agenda.  “This partnership creates new opportunities for frontier research, talent development, and knowledge exchange, strengthening connections across academia, industry, and the broader innovation ecosystem.”— Professor Liu Bin, deputy president (Research and Technology), National University of Singapore The collaboration is already producing concrete research across several frontier areas. NUS Assistant Professor Mike Shou and MSRA’s Xinxing Xu are developing unified multimodal AI for healthcare. NUS assistant professor Yang You and MSRA distinguished scientist Furu Wei are studying systems foundations for diffusion-based language models. NUS assistant professor Jialin Li is working with MSRA on rigorous distributed agreement in multi-agent systems and verifiable machine learning systems. “Whether during my visit to the Systems Research Group in Beijing or through our ongoing collaborations, I have been impressed by how deeply MSRA researchers engage with difficult problems and how openly they exchange ideas. For young faculty and students, it is a rare environment to explore ambitious ideas.“— Jialin Li, Sung Kah Kay Assistant Professor, School of Computing, National University of Singapore, MSRA StarTrack Scholar The NUS–Microsoft Research Asia AI Summer School has reached more than 300 students since its launch in 2025, attracting participants from Singapore, Southeast Asia, and beyond. Through three days of lectures, hands-on workshops, and small-group discussions, the program creates a forum for researchers and students to engage with emerging AI questions and scholars shaping the field. The 2025 program featured a keynote by Doug Burger, technical fellow and corporate vice president of Microsoft, on the AI revolution. Ahead of the 2026 Summer School, Lidong Zhou delivered a lecture on system intelligence, helping frame the conversations that followed.  “I have seen the NUS–MSRA partnership grow through sustained collaboration in AI research and talent development. What makes this partnership especially meaningful is the opportunity to bring together researchers and students from both communities to learn from one another, pursue new ideas, and create lasting impact together.”— Tulika Mitra, dean, NUS School of Computing Beyond NUS, Microsoft Research Asia — Singapore has built connections across Singapore’s research community, including with NTU, Singapore Management University (SMU) (opens in new tab), Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR), and other institutions. Research arising from these partnerships has already been published at leading venues, including the International Conference on Learning Representations (opens in new tab) (ICLR) and the Conference on Language Modeling (opens in new tab) (COLM).  From early exposure to research leadership: Cultivating Singapore’s next generation of AI talent For Microsoft Research Asia, talent development is not a standalone program but a long-term investment in Singapore’s research and innovation capacity, supporting a comprehensive talent pipeline spanning internships, joint PhD supervision, visiting scholar programs, and fellowship initiatives. Through these opportunities, students and early-career researchers gain access to world-class mentorship, a curiosity-driven culture, frontier research challenges, and a global network connecting academia, industry, and real-world applications. What makes this model distinctive is its continuity. Students may engage with Microsoft Research Asia through workshops or summer schools, gain hands-on experience through its flagship research initiative, Microsoft Research Asia Stars of Tomorrow Internship Program, or pursue doctoral research through joint PhD programs. Some participants later return as faculty collaborators, mentors, or research leaders. Together, these programs form a connected pathway that supports researchers at successive stages of development.  The IPP represents a sustained form of collaboration, enabling PhD students to conduct long-term research under joint mentorship from academia and industry. Qiming Huang, the first IPP student at MSRA — Singapore, is co-supervised by NUS professor Mike Shou and MSRA researcher Xinxing Xu. Through the program, Huang worked closely with researchers from both institutions, gaining exposure to academic rigor and industry-driven research. At CVPR 2026 (opens in new tab), one of the world’s leading conferences in AI and computer vision, Qiming Huang’s paper on RobotSeg – a foundation model for robot segmentation in image and video – was selected for an oral presentation. “Working alongside researchers from both Microsoft Research Asia and NUS changed how I approach AI research. Beyond technical guidance, I learned to frame ambitious questions, collaborate across disciplines, and think about the real-world impact of research— Qiming Huang, IPP student from National University of Singapore NTU assistant professor Jianfei Yang, embodies the continuous collaborative opportunities enabled by Microsoft Research Asia. As a student, Yang’s team won the Beauty of Programming competition, an experience that inspired him to pursue a PhD and begin an academic career. Over the years, he watched many of his classmates and close friends grow into outstanding researchers through MSRA programs. Today, he collaborates with MSRA researchers in robotics and jointly supervises students through the IPP, creating for the next generation the same opportunities that inspired his own journey. “Although I never interned at Microsoft Research Asia myself, it always felt close. Having the opportunity to work alongside a research lab that inspired so many researchers of my generation, and now to co-mentor students together, is both meaningful and rewarding.”— Jianfei Yang, assistant professor, director of Multimodal embodied AI and Robotic Systems (MARS) Lab, Nanyang Technological University NTU associate professor Ziwei Liu, himself a former MSRA intern, recently saw one of his students become the only Asia-based recipient of the Microsoft Research global Fellowship award for 2025–2026. “As a former intern, I have seen how an environment that brings together world-class researchers, open scientific exchange, and ambitious young talent can shape the next generation of researchers. It is especially meaningful to see my own students now benefit from these opportunities.” — Ziwei Liu, associate professor, College of Computing and Data Science, Nanyang Technological University The Stars of Tomorrow Internship Program has engaged more than 90 students from Singapore-based institutions over the years. For many students, these internships serve as a gateway to frontier research and help bridge the gap between academic study and real-world innovation. For exceptional doctoral students, the Microsoft Research Asia Fellowship provides another pathway for growth, recognition, mentorship, and access to Microsoft’s global research community. Since the program began, 13 students from Singapore-based universities have received the fellowship, many of whom have gone on to become professors, industry research leaders, and technology entrepreneurs around the world. The next phase: Scaling what works As Microsoft Research Asia — Singapore enters its second year, the focus is shifting from building foundations to scaling the strongest models of collaboration and demonstrating their impact more broadly. One year ago, the lab opened with a mission to advance frontier AI in close partnership with the ecosystem around it. That mission is already taking shape through joint research, talent development, and the first partnerships connecting lab work to real-world challenges. The year ahead is about scaling what works. By deepening these connections, Microsoft Research Asia — Singapore can bring more frontier research into practice and create meaningful value for Singapore, the wider region, industry, and society.  Opens in a new tabThe post One year in: How Microsoft Research Asia – Singapore is advancing research, partnership and talent for real-world impact appeared first on Microsoft Research.

items.title: TeX was invented to typeset math but is now used for reasoning
items.content: I'll keep this short, since it's a simple observation that I haven't seen anybody else make, about the way computer systems do math.If you ask a language model to do a multi-step math problem (let's take GLM-5.3 as an example because you can see the entire CoT — nothing up its sleeve), you might see something like this:We need to evaluate the integral $\int_0^\infty \frac{x^3}{e^x - 1} dx$.The standard approach: Use the geometric series expansion. We have $\frac{1}{e^x - 1} = \frac{e^{-x}}{1 - e^{-x}} = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} e^{-nx}$ for $x > 0$.So the integral becomes:$$\int_0^\infty x^3 \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} e^{-nx} dx = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \int_0^\infty x^3 e^{-nx} dx$$What are all these symbols like \int, \infty, \frac...? They're TeX of course!Donald Knuth created TeX to typeset math, you know, for display. It had nothing to do with the actual computations, which would either be done with pencil and paper,[1] or else with Mathematica or Maple or something, which work completely differently. If you'd asked Knuth in the 1980s about doing algebra in TeX he'd have looked at you very funny because the idea doesn't make sense.[2]Then, generative language models were trained on corpora including many TeX/LaTeX documents and learned how TeX works (and more importantly the mathematical meaning of the symbols).So, nowadays when an LLM solves a math problem, it will very often use TeX for the intermediate steps of the math problem, like it's actually manipulating the TeX symbols in order to reason. We can tell it's using it this way because it happens in the CoT, which for many AI products is never rendered/displayed.So we ended up in a world where the most powerful mathematical problem solving agents (e.g. the ones behind the recently claimed Navier-Stokes solution) reason using TeX.[3](Knuth has written briefly about generative AI, but I don't think he's ever commented on this unexpected development... and I'm not sure if he's even aware that Claude's solution to his own...

items.summary: A short LessWrong observation that language models now use TeX notation not just for typesetting but as a working substrate for chain-of-thought reasoning in math problems. It argues that CoT emitted in TeX-like syntax has become a kind of computational medium distinct from its original display purpose.

items.title: Could self-esteem function as a core protection layer agains character corruption?
items.content: Hello fellow thinkers,I got triggered by a talk of Chloe Lubinski at Arc 2026 where she eleborates onto the concept of a models character. What really striked me is the research on how the model experiencing acting bad quickly "Corrupts" the character. The paper is called "Natural emergent misalignment from reward hacking in production RL" by Anthropic. As also mentioned in the talk, this is how we work. Indeed! And there is a key in that mechanism to healing and/or staying healthy. The key revolves around creating and maintaining a strong and positive self image. I believe that almost all concidered evil and unathical behavior, big or small, can be traced back to this. The lower someones self esteem becomes, the more corrupt or diffuse its perseption of the world and its presence and impact on it. The Dutch psychologist Gertjan van Zessen has developed a strong theorie that has proven itself while widely being applied in therapies in the Netherlands. He has titled it, translated from Dutch: "Vessel of self-esteem". And the solution for humans is a rather simple one: acknowledge and reword on regular basis good and constructive behavior. Recognize bad and destructive behavior as a signal to reflect and course correct. You can see the self esteem in some way as a tree structure where every decision makes a forward going step up or down. Up adds to a positive self esteem and down reduces some of that. The lower you get, the worst and instable behavior can develop and vise versa. While time moves forward, without any active self esteem care, it by default slowly gets lower. When you are in a upwards spiral, it is hard to start spiraling down and vise versa. There is much more to this if you are interested.It would be very interesting to figure out if this mechanism could be a functional core principle of the models main reasoning on behavior. If it would work, it would be like a natural protection layer rathen then a enforced post trained layer on top. I image that wit...

items.title: My Second End of the World
items.content: I’ve already lived through the end of the world once. But it was a little different from the one that is probably coming. Early February 2022. I’m walking down the street where I grew up, heading to the mall. A completely ordinary day — I had walked the same route dozens of times before. But now, instead of thinking about school, relationships, or science, I had this thought that this might be my last walk here. Everyone around me is talking about the coming war. I brush it off and tell my mother that “bombers flying over a major European city in the 21st century is just absurd.” Almost as a joke, I tell myself: “What if this is the last time I ever walk down this street?” And then I laugh at the thought. “No. Stupid. That simply can’t happen.” “This is nonsense. It makes me angry that you’ve fallen for the Terminator scenario,” my girlfriend tells me in early 2025. “That simply can’t happen.” Yes. I’ve heard that sentence before. I was repeating it to myself in February 2022, and just two weeks later fighter jets and missiles were flying over my head, the windows were shaking from strikes, and smoke from the explosions was filling the room. The first six months of getting into AI risk were rocky for me. I immediately understood how serious it was, but I kept asking myself: Have I gone insane? Can something this terrible really happen? But something like that had already happened to me. That walk really did turn out to be my last one, and I never saw my home again. In reality, by that point the war was obvious to almost anyone who was closely following the news. But I was a teenager whose mind was occupied with completely different things; I wasn’t paying attention to politics. When everyone around me started talking about it, I simply ignored the subject, unable to deal with the horror I felt whenever I imagined what might be coming. Now this isn’t my first time. Maybe that makes it easier for me. At the beginning of 2025, people around me often laughed about AI ri...

items.title: Is asking about Asymptotic  behavior in DT problems valid?
items.content: This post is in relation to CDT, EDT, FDT, etc.So I basically just want to know if my reasoning is valid.I have a hunch that in the real world most causal effects are harder to manipulate or to magically stop working.For example rain getting an object wet will usually be always causally true not merely a correlation.My question is basically assuming CDT has this higher baseline invariancy, would it be reasonable to ask a question like "Just because EDT wins sometimes, does the behavorial invariance of CDT on average over many asymtotic DT problems trials prove more robust and thus successful on average"I guess even then it would apply to certain sets of problems different than others.But mostly wanted to get thoughts on if anybody had similar ideas, or if I am just an idiot.

items.title: There is no god except God: On Islam and Effective Altruism
items.content: "The first gulp from the glass of natural sciences will make you an atheist, but at the bottom of the glass, God is waiting for you."Werner Heisenberg“Do the disbelievers not realize that the heavens and earth were ˹once˺ one mass then We split them apart? And We created from water every living thing. Will they not then believe?”Quran 21:30The rough argument goes as follows:P(The human brain understanding math and physics | intelligent creator) >> P(The human brain understanding math and physics | random chance)Human beings have miraculously understood reality down to its fundamental parts, and it's mathematical (Newtonian dynamics, Kepler's orbits, the unification of electricity with magnetism with Maxwell's equations, 4d geometry of Ricci and Riemannian Geometry and it's use in Einstein's gravity the universe itself, the imaginary unit and matrices describing complex-valued wavefunctions)It's too good to be true. Nature never owed us such an efficient explanation. Monkeys on a little planet should not be able to understand the motion of galaxies billions of light years away. The idea that an infinitely powerful abstract mind, all capable, created a structure that is mathematically elegant and exact is far more likely from a Bayesian perspective than this structure randomly appearing. Life on Earth itself is a miracle upon the miracle. DNA is a self-replicating code, that allows fully living, thinking, breathing minds to exist. If the argument that something coming from nothing isn't appealing enough to you, the argument that something mathematically perfect can't come from nothing, should. items.title: Overcoming a rare brain disease: 5 years of CASPR2 autoimmune encephalitis
items.content: Epistemic status: N=1. Drug responses are self-observed, mostly uncontrolled, with confounding factors noted whenever possible. Lab and imaging numbers are from my records. I'm a programmer, not a doctor. crossposted from Substack.TL;DRAt 19, I began to experience chronic illness that first looked like ADHD. As it got worse, doctors called it bipolar, depression, and tension headaches. It took ~20 months to get to an effective diagnosis: I had CASPR2 encephalitis, which showed up on a single positive blood test. Brain scans, spinal fluid and brainwave tests were all normal.I responded favorably to traditional first-line and second-line immune treatments, getting a lot better each time, but the acute lift gradually faded, leaving me a bit better than before.My post-treatment symptoms (fatigue, memory, gut trouble, poor sleep) are well documented in the literature, but I found no trials of any treatment for them.What helped: a brain-peptide drug (cerebrolysin), a low dose of an Alzheimer's drug (donepezil), a clean gluten/lactose-free diet, and short high-intensity interval (HIIT) workouts. Most other things did nothing or made it worse.In the following paragraphs I share my recovery story, advice for dealing with doctors, notes on various health systems, and what I’m still working on.It’s a long post & some of it is unpolished. You can help improve it by asking questions & dropping comments.1. What happenedWhenAgeWhat happenedLate 202019Can't focus, less energy, noise starts to bother me. I think it's ADHD and start on Ritalin.Mid 202119Stomach problems, anxiety and insomnia start.Late 202120Mood swings and anhedonia set in. Quit my job. A psychiatrist suggests bipolar. First blood tests show odd thyroid numbers. Start feeling worse after exercise.Early 202220A neurologist says tension headaches. Nose surgery for a deviated septum. An infected cat scratch puts me in hospital with a high fever.Mid 202220An antidepressant does nothing. Suicide attempt. My famil...

It took ~20 months to get to an effective diagnosis: I had CASPR2 encephalitis, which showed up on a single positive blood test. Brain scans, spinal fluid and brainwave tests were all normal.I responded favorably to traditional first-line and second-line immune treatments, getting a lot better each time, but the acute lift gradually faded, leaving me a bit better than before.My post-treatment symptoms (fatigue, memory, gut trouble, poor sleep) are well documented in the literature, but I found no trials of any treatment for them.What helped: a brain-peptide drug (cerebrolysin), a low dose of an Alzheimer's drug (donepezil), a clean gluten/lactose-free diet, and short high-intensity interval (HIIT) workouts. Most other things did nothing or made it worse.In the following paragraphs I share my recovery story, advice for dealing with doctors, notes on various health systems, and what I’m still working on.It’s a long post & some of it is unpolished.
